358.title: The blind men and the elephant
358.hook: each man touches one part of the elephant and quarrels with the rest (Udana 6.4)
358.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the story of the blind men and the elephant to warn against clinging to partial views and quarreling over them, and it is widely told in other traditions too.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stoicism, a neighbor to this path, with a similar calm and different reasons. Your line: same calm, different reasons.

Year two began with an elephant's footprint. Right view ends with the whole elephant. In the city of Savatthi, the monks come back from their alms round shaken. All over town, teachers and their followers are arguing about the big questions: is the world eternal, is the soul the body. Each side says only this is true, everything else is foolish. The arguing has turned into shouting, and the shouting into wounding words. The monks tell the Buddha. He doesn't declare a winner. He tells them about a king who once borrowed an elephant.
screen: `MONKS COME BACK SHAKEN.` → `ONLY THIS IS TRUE.` → `A KING BORROWS AN ELEPHANT.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Udana, a short book of inspired sayings, chapter six. Long ago, the Buddha says, a king of Savatthi had his servant gather every man in the city who had been born blind. Then he had an elephant brought, and let each man touch one part: the head, the ear, the tusk, the trunk, the body, the foot, the back, the tail, the tuft at the end of the tail. Then the king asked: what is an elephant like? Those who touched the head said: like a water pot. The ear: a winnowing basket. The tusk: a plowshare. The trunk: a plow pole. The body: a storehouse. The foot: a post. The back: a mortar. The tail: a pestle. The tuft: a broom. And then, the text says, they began to argue, each insisting the elephant is like this, not like that, until they came to blows. And the king was delighted. The quarreling teachers are like this, the Buddha says: they don't see the whole, and so they fight over the part. The story is aimed at anyone, of any group, who seizes a part and calls it the whole, including his own monks. The big questions in the background are the same ones Malunkyaputta wanted answered, the ones left aside in the arrow story. This story has neighbors: Jains, Hindus and Sufi poets like Rumi tell their own versions, each with its own lesson. In the Udana, the lesson closes the section on right view: each holds a part.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a view held by someone you disagree with, not to adopt it, just to touch it, and ask: what part of the elephant might they be holding, and what did they touch that I didn't? If irritation comes, notice it, and come back to the breath. Let both your part and theirs be parts.
Jaccandha, born blind. Each touches one part of the elephant and fights over the whole: the Buddha's picture of clinging to partial views.
Your line: each holds a part. No single hand covers the whole elephant. That's day three hundred fifty-eight.

359.title: Right intention
359.hook: intentions of letting go, of goodwill, of harmlessness (MN 117)
359.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers commonly present right intention through its three parts, renunciation, goodwill and harmlessness, and students may set an intention at the start of a day, a meditation or a retreat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jaccandha, the blind men and the elephant. Your line: each holds a part.

Two people hand you a cup of coffee. Same cup, same coffee, same smile. One cares whether your morning goes well. The other wants something from you this afternoon. From the outside, there's no difference at all. From the inside, they're walking two different roads. That inside part, the aim behind the act, is the second spoke of the wheel. After right view comes the question: now that you see, what are you aiming at?
screen: `TWO CUPS OF COFFEE.` → `SAME CUP, DIFFERENT AIM.` → `WHAT ARE YOU AIMING AT?`

segments.voice: The Pali is samma sankappa. Sankappa means thought, intention, resolve: what the mind is set on. Rhys Davids, translating the first sermon, called it right aspirations. The suttas, in the Great Forty and in the sutta that lists all eight factors, define it in three parts: the intention of letting go, of goodwill, and of harmlessness. Letting go, nekkhamma, is the aim of wanting less, of not being run by craving. Goodwill is wishing others well instead of ill. Harmlessness is the aim of not causing pain, which teachers link with compassion. Each aim is the medicine for a poison: letting go for greed, goodwill for ill will, harmlessness for cruelty. Notice where right intention sits. With right view, it makes up the training in wisdom. Isn't intention about will, not wisdom? But in the way the path is taught, seeing clearly and aiming well belong together: someone who sees that craving brings dukkha begins to aim away from it. And look at the order of the list. Speech, action and livelihood come after intention. The aim is set before the mouth opens or the hand moves. Right intention isn't a promise to be perfect. It's choosing the aim behind the cup of coffee.

segments.voice: Choose one of the three aims, letting go, goodwill or harmlessness, and let it become a short phrase in your own words: today, I'll want a little less; or, today, I'll wish people well; or, today, I won't add to anyone's pain. Breathe it in and out a few times, not as a vow, just pointing the compass.
Samma sankappa. Right intention: aiming at letting go, at goodwill, and at harmlessness. The second factor of the path.
Your line: intend it. The aim is set before the hand moves. See you tomorrow.

360.title: Two piles
360.hook: before his awakening he sorted his thoughts into two kinds (MN 19)
360.carry: a path worn across a field
360.howItsDone: Some Buddhist meditation teachers teach students to notice thoughts as wholesome or unwholesome and to see where they lead, a method drawn from the Dvedhavitakka Sutta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma sankappa, right intention, with its three aims: letting go, goodwill, harmlessness. Your line: intend it.

Cleaning out a closet usually comes down to two piles: keep, and let go. You pick up a sweater, hold it for a second, and drop it on one side or the other. It's slow at first. After an hour you're fast, because your hands have learned what belongs where. In one sutta the Buddha looks back to the years before his awakening, when he was still searching, and tells the monks about a simple experiment he ran on his own mind. Two piles.
screen: `CLEANING OUT A CLOSET.` → `KEEP, AND LET GO.` → `AN EXPERIMENT ON HIS OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: The sutta is number nineteen in the Middle-Length Discourses, and its name means two kinds of thought. Before my awakening, the Buddha says, while I was still a bodhisatta, it occurred to me: what if I divide my thoughts into two classes? On one side, thoughts of sensual desire, of ill will, and of cruelty. On the other: thoughts of letting go, of goodwill, and of harmlessness. That second pile is exactly yesterday's right intention. Then he watched. When a thought from the first pile came up, he saw where it led: to his own affliction, to others' affliction, to both. It blocked wisdom and led away from peace. And as he considered that, the sutta says, the thought subsided, and he let it go. A thought from the second pile led to no one's harm, and helped wisdom grow. Then comes a line worth carrying home. Whatever someone keeps thinking about and pondering, the Buddha says, that becomes the leaning of their mind. Think often about ill will, and the mind leans toward ill will. Think often about goodwill, and it leans toward goodwill. Like a path worn across a field, or a closet that sorts itself faster every time. The method is humble. No special state required. Just noticing which pile a thought belongs in, and where it's heading. A practice from before the awakening, offered to anyone.
screen: `BEFORE MY AWAKENING.` · `DESIRE, ILL WILL, CRUELTY.` · `WHERE DOES THIS THOUGHT LEAD?` · `WHAT YOU PONDER, THE MIND LEANS TO.` · then, large: `TWO PILES.`

segments.voice: Watch thoughts come and go, and as each one passes, set it gently on a side: wanting, resentment or harm in the first pile; letting go, goodwill or kindness in the second. If you can't tell, let it pass unsorted. Don't argue with any thought; just notice which way it leans.
Two piles. The Buddha's practice before awakening: sorting thoughts into those that lead to harm and those that lead to good, because the mind leans toward what it ponders.
Your line: a path worn across a field. What the mind keeps returning to, it leans toward. That's day three hundred sixty.

361.title: The cowherd in autumn
361.hook: a cowherd guards the ripe crops with a stick, then rests under a tree once the harvest is in (MN 19)
361.howItsDone: Meditation teachers often describe a balance of effort and ease, sometimes using the cowherd of MN 19: careful guarding of the mind at first, then relaxed awareness once the mind has settled.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two piles, the Buddha sorting his thoughts by where they lead. Your line: a path worn across a field. Today, the same sutta, and its cowherd.
screen: `TWO PILES — A PATH WORN ACROSS A FIELD.`

segments.voice: Late in the rains, the crops stand tall and green right up to the edge of the village paths. It's beautiful, and for a cowherd it's a nightmare. His cows want nothing more than to wander into those fields and eat. If they do, he could be beaten, locked up, fined or blamed. So all day long he walks beside them with a stick, tapping and turning them back. Then the harvest comes in, the fields are bare, and everything changes. In the sutta of two kinds of thought, the Buddha says his mind was like those cows.
screen: `THE CROPS STAND TALL.` → `COWS WANT THE FIELDS.` → `A COWHERD WITH A STICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the first season, from the Middle-Length Discourses, number nineteen. In the last month of the rains, in autumn, when the crops are ripening, a cowherd guards his cows by tapping and poking them this way and that with a stick, because he sees the trouble that will come if they stray into the crops. In the same way, the Buddha says, he saw the danger in unwholesome thoughts, and the blessing in letting them go. That's the guarding: yesterday's two piles, done with attention, the stick tapping when the mind wanders toward ill will or craving. Then something surprising. Even wholesome thinking, he says, if he kept it up too long, would tire his body, and a tired body strains the mind. So he steadied his mind inside, quieted it, and brought it together. Now the second season. In the last month of the hot season, when all the crops have been brought into the village, the cowherd guards his cows while sitting at the foot of a tree or out in the open. He only needs to be aware: there are the cows. No stick. No running. That, the Buddha says, was all he needed then: simple awareness that those states were there. Two lessons sit in this one picture. Guarding the mind takes effort at the start, and that's fine. But effort isn't the whole path. There comes a time to put the stick down and rest under the tree, still aware, but at ease.

segments.voice: For the first half of the sit, be the cowherd in autumn: watch the breath closely, and each time the mind wanders, tap it gently back. Then let the stick go, as if sitting at the foot of a tree with the fields bare, and simply know: there's the breath, there are the thoughts. Nothing to herd; just aware, and at ease.
Gopalaka, a cowherd. Guarding the mind with care while the crops are ripe, then resting under a tree, simply aware, once the harvest is in.
Your line: guard, then rest. Effort has its season, and so does ease. Day three hundred sixty-one, done.

362.title: Letting go
362.hook: renunciation as the relief of wanting less, not grim denial
362.howItsDone: Buddhists practice letting go in small doses: on observance days lay people may keep eight precepts, skipping the evening meal and entertainment, and in some Theravada countries men may ordain as monks for a short time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gopalaka, the cowherd with his stick, and then at rest under a tree. Your line: guard, then rest.

Moving day. The twelfth box comes down the stairs, and inside are chargers for phones nobody in the house has owned in years. The whole box goes in the donation bin, and something odd can happen. The shoulders come down. The body feels lighter, and not only in the arms. Nobody would call that grim, or a sacrifice. It's closer to relief. That, in miniature, is the first thought in the Buddha's good pile, and its usual English translation can mislead.
screen: `THE TWELFTH BOX.` → `DROPPED AT THE BIN.` → `THE SHOULDERS COME DOWN.`

segments.voice: The word is nekkhamma, usually translated renunciation, and renunciation sounds like a monk in a cold cell refusing soup. In the suttas the word can point to going forth, leaving home to become a monk or nun. But it also names a thought anyone can have: the thought of putting something down. In the sutta of the two kinds of thought, letting go comes first in the good pile, ahead of goodwill and not harming. Here's the honest part. In another sutta, a householder named Tapussa tells Ananda that letting go looks, to people like him, like a cliff edge. Ananda takes him to the Buddha, whose answer is candid. Before his awakening, he says, he too thought renunciation was good, yet his heart didn't leap at it. It only did once he had truly seen the trouble that wanting brings, and tasted the ease of not wanting. So the tradition doesn't say grit your teeth. It says look closely until the relief becomes real to you. The Dhammapada frames it as a trade, in Max Müller's words: "If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great." And nekkhamma isn't only for monks. Theravada tradition counts it among the perfections, and some lay people practice it in small doses, keeping eight precepts on an observance day. Less, chosen freely, can feel like more room.
screen: `NEKKHAMMA: THE THOUGHT OF PUTTING DOWN.` · `FIRST IN THE GOOD PILE.` · `TAPUSSA: IT LOOKS LIKE A CLIFF.` · `LOOK UNTIL THE RELIEF IS REAL.` · then, large: `THE RELIEF OF LESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small, live want, the next snack, the reply to a message, a purchase waiting in a cart, and notice how it sits in the body: a lean forward, a little tightness somewhere. Now, just for these two minutes, put it down; you can pick it up later if you choose. Watch what the body does when you set it down, and if there's any relief, rest in it.
Nekkhamma. Letting go, renunciation: the thought of putting something down, first in the good pile, felt as relief rather than loss.
Your line: the relief of less. Letting go can feel like setting down a heavy box. Until tomorrow.

363.title: Goodwill
363.hook: the intention of non-ill-will: metta as a steering wheel
363.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions practice mettā, often by repeating short phrases of goodwill toward themselves, loved ones, strangers and difficult people; many monastics recite the simile of the saw as a reminder of patience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nekkhamma, letting go, felt as relief rather than loss. Your line: the relief of less.

In the city of Savatthi, the Buddha says, there lived a lady of the house named Vedehika, and everyone said so: so gentle, so calm, so peaceful. Her maid, Kali, wondered whether that was true, or whether Vedehika had simply never been given a reason to be otherwise. So Kali tested her. One morning she got up late. Vedehika scowled. The next morning, later still: sharp words. The third morning Kali slept in again, and her famously gentle mistress grabbed a rolling pin and hit her on the head. Kali ran out bleeding and told the whole street.
screen: `SO GENTLE, EVERYONE SAID.` → `THE MAID SLEEPS IN.` → `THE THIRD MORNING.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells that story in the sutta of the simile of the saw, and his point is sharp: a person is gentle only until disagreeable words reach them. Being calm when nobody pushes doesn't prove much. That's why the second right intention is goodwill. In Pali it's abyāpāda, literally non-ill-will, and the suttas fill it in with mettā, loving-kindness. Not a warm feeling that washes over you when it likes. An intention: a direction you set. Think of a steering wheel. The road throws things at you: a rude email, a driver who cuts in, a relative who says the thing. You don't control the road. You do have your hands on the wheel, and goodwill is which way you turn it. The same sutta then goes about as far as a teaching can go. Even if bandits were to cut you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, the Buddha says, anyone whose mind filled with hate would not be carrying out his teaching. He tells the monks to train so their minds stay unshaken, they speak no evil words, and they stay with goodwill toward that very person, and from there toward the whole world. Most of us will never meet those bandits. We'll meet the slow line at the pharmacy and the group chat. That may be why the same sutta opens with Vedehika and closes with the saw. The test usually comes in small, ordinary pushes, and each one is a turn of the wheel.
screen: `GENTLE UNTIL SOMEONE PUSHES.` · `ABYĀPĀDA: NON-ILL-WILL.` · `GOODWILL IS A STEERING WHEEL.` · `EVEN UNDER THE SAW.` · then, large: `STEER BY GOODWILL.`

segments.voice: Think of a conversation you'll probably have today with a little friction in it, and picture the moment where it usually goes sideways. Rest your hands lightly, as if on a wheel, and set the direction before it begins: whatever they say, turn toward their good, not agreeing with everything, just the direction. If the old irritation shows up in the picture, notice it, and turn the wheel gently back.
Goodwill. Abyāpāda, non-ill-will, the second kind of right intention: not a mood but a direction you set, close kin to mettā.

364.title: Harmlessness
364.hook: the intention not to harm, even in thought
364.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists take the first precept, not to kill, as the outward form of harmlessness; some also reflect on verses like Dhammapada 129 or practice compassion meditation toward beings who suffer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: goodwill, a direction you set, even when someone pushes. Your line: steer by goodwill. Today ends the week.

Credit for an idea gets taken in a meeting, and on the drive home a little film starts to play. In it, the person who took it trips on the stairs. Their coffee spills down their shirt. Their car gets a flat in the rain. Nobody is badly hurt, of course. Just enough. Nobody acts on it. A film like that can run for a long time before anyone notices it's running. The Buddha noticed. Before his awakening, he says, he caught thoughts of harming in his own mind and put them in the bad pile, right beside ill will. Today, the last of the three right intentions: harmlessness, all the way down into thought.
screen: `CREDIT TAKEN IN A MEETING.` → `A LITTLE FILM STARTS.` → `JUST ENOUGH HARM.`

segments.voice: The word on our list is ahimsa, a word Pali and Sanskrit share: the not-harming that Jains and Hindus hold dear as well. In the Pali list of right intentions, the word is avihiṃsā, non-cruelty: the intention not to harm. Goodwill was about not wishing ill. This one leans closer to action: not wanting anyone to suffer, and not wanting to be the cause. In the sutta of the two kinds of thought, when a thought of harming arose in him, the Buddha saw that it led to his own affliction, to others', or to both, and away from wisdom. As he considered that, it subsided. So harm starts upstream, in the film, long before a hand moves. The Dhammapada gives the reason in one line, in Max Müller's words: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." You are like them. That's the whole argument. A later verse says a person isn't called noble for injuring living creatures, but for having pity on all of them. Later teachers pair harmlessness with compassion, karuṇā: it's the soil compassion grows in. Look back at the week. The blind men, each holding a part. Intend it. Two piles. Guard, then rest. The relief of less. Steer by goodwill. And today, no harm meant. Three right intentions, one direction.
screen: `AVIHIṂSĀ: THE INTENTION NOT TO HARM.` · `HARM STARTS UPSTREAM.` · `YOU ARE LIKE THEM.` · `THE SOIL COMPASSION GROWS IN.` · then, large: `NO HARM MEANT.`

segments.voice: Gently look for the film: is there anyone you've been quietly wishing a small misfortune on, a coworker, a neighbor, someone on the news? Don't scold yourself for finding it; just catch it, the way you'd catch a glass before it hits the floor. Then do what the Dhammapada suggests, remember they're like you, they flinch at pain too, and let the film stop there.
Ahimsa. Not harming. In the Buddha's list it's avihiṃsā, the intention not to harm, the third right intention.
Your line: no harm meant. A film can end unfinished. One more week on the path, complete.
